analysis.one_liner: Opens federal employee health plans to all Americans with sliding-scale tax credits for premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2004 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; the Congress ended in January 2005 with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Barbara Boxer proposed letting any American who isn't already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, or a federal plan buy into the same health plans offered to federal employees. Premiums would be paid by enrollees — with no government contribution — but a refundable tax credit would cover the full premium for people below the poverty line, stepping down to nothing for those above four times poverty. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be the roughly tens of millions of Americans without job-based health insurance: anyone not eligible for Medicare, Medicaid, or federal coverage could buy into the federal employees' health plan menu, and low-income families would have had most or all of their premium covered by a refundable tax credit paid directly to the insurer. Private insurance carriers would also have gained, since they would be contracted to offer these new plans and could be compelled to do so as a condition of keeping their lucrative federal-employee contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured working families and private insurers

how_it_helps.text: It would open the Federal Employees Health Benefits program's private plans to any American not already covered by a public program, Medicare, or federal coverage, so people without job-based insurance could buy the same menu of plans federal workers get.

Families below the poverty line would get a refundable tax credit covering 100% of their premium, with the share stepping down as income rises — 65% up to twice poverty, 40% up to three times, 30% up to four times — and the credit is refundable, so even households owing no income tax would get it.
Low-income enrollees would not have to wait for a tax refund: the Treasury would send advance payments directly to the plan on their behalf.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the Treasury, which would fund the refundable premium credits, including advance payments made directly to insurers on behalf of low-income enrollees; enrollees above the subsidy range would pay their own premiums, and carriers would bear the risk of a new individual-market pool that the bill kept separate from federal employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via premium tax credits

drawbacks.text: The government would pay nothing toward these premiums; the only help is the sliding-scale tax credit, and anyone above 400% of poverty gets no credit at all, leaving middle-income buyers to pay the full private premium.

Enrollees would be kept in a risk pool separate from federal employees, so this pool — likely including many people buying insurance individually because they were already sick or had no employer coverage — would bear its own costs, and the bill allows premiums to vary by region.

The bill excludes anyone 65 or older or eligible for public programs like Medicare or Medicaid, so it would not have covered the populations with the hardest time getting care, and the bill set no overall spending limit or financing plan for the new tax credits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — letting anyone buy the same plans federal workers get, with a full subsidy for the poor — was real and aimed directly at the uninsured. But the bill was lean by design: no government contribution to premiums, a separate risk pool that would hold mostly higher-cost individual buyers, regional price variation, and subsidies that vanished above four times the poverty line. It would have helped mainly the working poor and near-poor, not solved the broader coverage problem, and its cost to the Treasury was left undefined. It was a modest, private-carrier-based approach — and it still never got even a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on March 3, 2004, the same day it was introduced.
The complete action history shows no further action of any kind — the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill was designed to route coverage through private carriers under contract with the Office of Personnel Management, not to create a government-run health plan, and it barred any government contribution toward premiums.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the status quo, with no new obligation to offer individual plans as a condition of federal-employee contracts; the low-income uninsured gained nothing, since the subsidies never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 3, 2004.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee chaired by Republicans in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 3, 2004 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, no Republican support, and died without action in the Finance Committee, then chaired by a Republican, during a Republican-controlled Congress.

industries.note: The bill does not create a government-run insurer; the Office of Personnel Management would contract with private carriers, and it could force any carrier wanting a lucrative federal-employee plan to also offer these new individual plans. Insurers would gain millions of subsidized premium-paying customers while remaining the channel through which the coverage flows.

industries.industry: Employers who do not offer health coverage
industries.note: Employees without employer coverage could instead buy subsidized individual plans, giving some workers an alternative to employer-based insurance; employers offering no coverage would feel less pressure to start.
